row: | DOC-A.1-14 | **CALL statement — runtime resources that are checked**, §14.9.4.4 GR3c, required + documented | **The set of runtime resources checked is EMPTY, so a CALL never raises EC-PROGRAM-RESOURCES.** COBOL.NET checks no runtime resource beyond locating the program (§14.9.4.4 GR3b), and a failure to locate it is “the program cannot be located”: a callee is located when it is registered in the run unit's program table — compiled into the calling assembly, or a separately compiled module `<name>.dll` in the application directory whose `__CobolModule.Register()` registrar has run (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule`; the rest of the locating mechanics are implementor-defined, see items 15 and 16). A module file that exists but cannot be loaded (a truncated or foreign image, or a dependency the registrar itself needs) or whose registrar throws has therefore NOT been located, and the CALL takes GR3b's arm: **EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND**, the call is not successful, and execution continues per GR3h (ON EXCEPTION, or the checking-state disposition). Once a program is located no further resource is checked before control transfers (GR3g). This follows GnuCOBOL under CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence — libcob's resolver sets EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND when a module is found but cannot be loaded, and has no EC-PROGRAM-RESOURCES raise site on CALL — except that GnuCOBOL also prints a runtime warning naming the module's path, which COBOL.NET does not issue. The same determination serves a user-defined function (item 89) and the class of an invoked method (item 102). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-20 | **Case mapping (compile-time, of the COBOL character repertoire)**, §8.1.3.2 GR1 with GR3 b) and GR4 b), required + documented | **COBOL.NET's compile-time case mapping IS Annex C (C.2 General case mappings) of the edition being compiled, applied as a fold from uppercase to lowercase** — the Unicode simple lowercase mapping of the Annex B characters that the A.1 item 20 NOTE recommends (C.2's own NOTE: the Changes_When_Lowercased property, Unicode 13.0.0). **Basic letters:** A–Z fold to a–z everywhere outside the non-hexadecimal forms of alphanumeric and national literals (§8.1.3.2 GR3 a/b), so `WS-Total` and `ws-total` are one word. **Extended letters** (A.4.6, claimed in §5): an uppercase extended letter folds to the lowercase letter C.2 pairs it with, and a letter C.2 does not list folds to nothing but itself (GR4 b), so `CAFÉ` and `café` are one word while dotless `ı` (U+0131) is distinct from `i` at COBOL 2023. The per-edition differences follow the annex: COBOL 2023 deletes `(0131,0069)` and `(03C2,03C3)` (E.2 item 14) and adds the E.3.3 item 6 pairs, so a 2002/2014 compilation folds by the older list. Today every name comparison uses the .NET ordinal-ignore-case comparison, which is identical to C.2 on A–Z. This compile-time mapping governs COBOL WORDS only; the RUNTIME mapping of the UPPER-CASE / LOWER-CASE functions is the separate §3 determination (the .NET invariant tables, or a locale's LC_CTYPE), and DOC-A.1-43's currency-symbol equivalence is its own rule. ⚠ **Not yet what the compiler does for extended letters:** the lexer admits only basic letters in a COBOL word, so every extended letter is rejected before any fold, and the ONE Annex C folding function that must key every name table (data-, procedure-, program-, file-, condition-names and the rest) does not exist yet (kb/Work PB1402); the basic-letter half holds today. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-23 | **Characters prohibited from use in text-words in COPY … REPLACING and REPLACE**, §7.2.2.5 rule 3, required + documented | **NONE — COBOL.NET prohibits no character in, or as, a text-word.** Any character of the compile-time coded character set (UTF-16, DOC-A.1-25) that is not a separator is an ordinary text-word character, whether or not it is in the COBOL character repertoire: `==éVAL==`, `==@Y~==` and `==€X==` are pseudo-text operands like any other and match exactly the text-words they spell, in both COPY … REPLACING and REPLACE, at every edition. What bounds a text-word is the §8.3.5 separator set (with the §7.2.2.5 rule 1 colon and parenthesis cases), the end of a source line, and the horizontal tab U+0009, which COBOL.NET treats as white space throughout source text as GnuCOBOL does (item 157) — and nothing else, so a character that merely LOOKS like a space but is not the COBOL character space — U+00A0 NO-BREAK SPACE, U+2000–U+200A, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, U+0085 — is a text-word character, and `==P<U+00A0>Q==` is ONE text-word that matches `P<U+00A0>Q` and never the two words `P Q`. Whether the text that results from replacement is a legal COBOL word is decided afterwards by the ordinary lexical rules, not by the text-manipulation pass. ⚠ **Not yet what the compiler does for the look-alike spaces:** `CopyProcessor.TokenizeTextWords` bounds text-words with `char.IsWhiteSpace`, so every other Unicode White_Space character (U+00A0, U+2000–U+200A, U+3000, U+0085, …) acts as a separator during matching (kb/Work PB1543); every other non-repertoire character already behaves as stated. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-25 | **COBOL character repertoire — encoding of, mapping of, substitute graphics**, §8.1.3.2 GR1 and GR5, required + documented | **Mapping:** every basic letter, basic digit, basic special character and extended letter maps to its ISO/IEC 10646 code point, held as UTF-16 — one coded character set serves both the alphanumeric and the national class, so the two share one numbering and GR1's alphanumeric-to-national correspondence is the identity (`A` is U+0041 in both; the figurative and editing values are item 32's row). **Encoding of source text:** decided per file (item 26's row): a byte-order mark selects UTF-8, UTF-16LE/BE or UTF-32, and a file with no mark is read as UTF-8. **A file with no mark that is not well-formed UTF-8 is read as ISO/IEC 8859-1 instead** — every byte is the character with that code point, so no source byte is lost or altered (a 0xE9 byte in `VALUE "A<0xE9>B"` is `é`, U+00E9, `FUNCTION ORD` 234) — and the compiler issues a WARNING naming the file, so the choice is never silent. **A file whose byte-order mark names an encoding its content is not well-formed in** (invalid UTF-8 after `EF BB BF`, a lone surrogate in UTF-16, a UTF-32 unit beyond U+10FFFF) **is a compile-time ERROR naming the file and the byte offset** — there is no fallback for a marked file, because the mark states the encoding. No source character is ever replaced by U+FFFD or any other stand-in. This is the byte-preserving disposition GnuCOBOL takes under CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence (cobc runs no conversion on source text, so each byte is one character with that byte's code). **Substitute graphics:** none; every character of the COBOL repertoire has its own graphic in ISO/IEC 10646, so GR5 never applies. The same at every edition. ⚠ **Not yet what the compiler does for malformed source text:** `CompilationInputs.ReadAllText` (`File.ReadAllText`) replaces each invalid byte sequence with U+FFFD and says nothing (`FUNCTION ORD` 65534), in literals, comments and library text alike, and whether or not the file has a byte-order mark (kb/Work PB1397); the mapping and BOM-selected encodings already behave as stated. | — |

record.notes: Rule: A.1 item 25 'COBOL character repertoire (encoding of, mapping of, substitute graphics) ... required ... documented (8.1.3; 8.1.3 GR1 and 5)'. cite.py --check 8.1.3.2 "The implementor shall define a mapping of each basic letter, basic digit, basic special character, and extended letter" -> OK §8.1.3.2 1) (General rules). cite.py --check 8.1.3.2 "substitute graphics may be specified by the implementor to replace the characters not represented" -> OK §8.1.3.2 5). cite.py --check 8.3.3.2.3 "Character-1 may be any character in the coded character set that the implementor has chosen for source code representation" -> OK §8.3.3.2.3 2) (Syntax rules). Determination reasoning: ISO leaves the mapping and the source encoding to the implementor (GR1) but a literal may hold only characters of the chosen source set (8.3.3.2.3 SR2); U+FFFD substitution silently changes a literal's content, so it is not a choice to document (PB1535). Two candidate fixes were on the table in PB1397 step 3 — a strict decoder with an error, or byte pass-through. Rule-1 precedence settles it: GnuCOBOL (next after ISO) accepts such source and preserves each byte as one character (no iconv on source), so rejecting it would be less conforming to the precedence than preserving it; in a UTF-16 repertoire the unique byte-preserving decoding is ISO/IEC 8859-1 (code point = byte, so FUNCTION ORD equals GnuCOBOL's byte+1 for every such byte). Whole-file (not per-sequence) fallback keeps DOC-A.1-26's one-encoding-per-file model; the warning keeps a CP1252 source (0x80 -> U+0080, not €) from being reinterpreted invisibly. PARTIAL: the ISO 10646/UTF-16 mapping and the BOM-selected encodings hold (DOC-A.1-26 probe, item 32/74 goldens); the malformed-UTF-8 arm diverges (probe). Owning defect kb/Work PB1397 (open, keeps DOC-A.1-25 per its step-3 section). The fix: CompilationInputs.ReadAllText detects BOM itself, decodes with UTF8Encoding(throwOnInvalidBytes: true), on DecoderFallbackException re-decodes the file as Latin-1 and records a warning (needs an allocated COBOLNET code). Witness needed: a golden reading a no-BOM file with a raw 0xE9 in a literal, expecting DISPLAY é and ORD 234 plus the warning in .err. Row stays GAP until then. row: | DOC-A.1-31 | **Computer's coded character set — the characters in and the encoding of the alphanumeric and national coded character sets, and the encoding for USAGE DISPLAY and USAGE NATIONAL**, §8.1.2 (with §8.3.3.2.3 SR2 and §8.3.3.5.3 SR2 for source representation), required + documented | **ONE coded character set serves both classes: the UTF-16 Basic Multilingual Plane, one code unit per character position** (the standing UTF-16 repertoire decision, applied in kb/Work R48's second section; items 33, 188). The alphanumeric and the national coded character set each contain all 65,536 BMP code units; a character outside the BMP is a surrogate pair occupying two character positions (§8.5.1.4, item 213). **In memory** every character is its UTF-16 code unit, whatever the item's class. **USAGE NATIONAL** is two bytes per character position, the code unit most significant byte first (UTF-16BE, item 213). **USAGE DISPLAY** is one byte per character position in ISO/IEC 8859-1 (item 209): a character U+0000–U+00FF is the byte of the same value, so the 256 characters U+0000–U+00FF are the ones with a DISPLAY byte image. **A character above U+00FF has no DISPLAY byte image, and COBOL.NET never loses it silently.** At an in-memory byte channel (the storage image read by CONVERT's ANY, HEX and BYTE legs, a REDEFINES or group image) it becomes `?` (0x3F) and EC-DATA-CONVERSION is set (item 33's decided disposition). At a FILE with no CODE-SET clause — record sequential, line sequential and report files alike (owner decision kb/Work R47) — the WRITE or REWRITE of a record area holding one is UNSUCCESSFUL, nothing reaches the medium, and the record area is unchanged: I-O status `'71'` for a line sequential file (§9.1.13.10; the character is outside the line sequential character set, item 115), `'91'` for every other sequential file and for a report file (§9.1.13.11; item 110). Reading needs no rule: every byte read decodes to U+0000–U+00FF. A CODE-SET clause selects the medium encoding instead (§5 row 27). **Source representation:** a source file is read as UTF-8 unless a byte-order mark names UTF-16 or UTF-32 (ISO/IEC 8859-1 when it has no mark and is not well-formed UTF-8, item 25), and every source character is designated a character of both compile-time sets, so an alphanumeric or a national literal may contain any BMP character; the compile-time and runtime sets are the same (item 34), e.g. `FUNCTION ORD("€")` is 8365. Every edition (the national set from 2002). ⚠ Diverges today: a WRITE of a record holding U+20AC puts `?` on the medium with status `'00'`, record and line sequential alike (kb/Work PB690). | `conformance:2002/l1c01_native_ordinal_positions_wide`; `conformance:2002/pb59_repertoire_identity` |

row: | DOC-A.1-39 | **CONTINUE statement — precision and maximum size of the AFTER interval**, §14.9.9.4 GR1, required + documented | **m = 0, n = 5, and the maximum meaningful value is 86,400 seconds (one day)** (`CobolTiming.MaxSeconds`). The interval behaves as a temporary `9(5)` item with no decimal places: a value of arithmetic-expression-1 **greater than 86,400 — however large, in any arithmetic mode and whatever the expression's form (literal, data item, product, quotient, power) — puts 86,400 in the temporary**, so the program is suspended for one day and never for less; any other value is stored by the implicit COMPUTE without ROUNDED, so a fraction truncates toward zero (`CONTINUE AFTER 1.9 SECONDS` suspends 1 second, `0.999…` suspends none). A value below zero is set to 0 and, with FC-CONTINUE-LESS-THAN-ZERO checking enabled, raises the nonfatal EC-CONTINUE-LESS-THAN-ZERO (GR1 a–c). Because m = 0, the processor-dependent fractional precision of Annex A.3 item 8 is not claimed (§2 row 8). COBOL 2023 only (CONTINUE AFTER is new in 2023). ⚠ **Not yet what the compiler does for an interval whose value, or a product inside it, reaches the carrier's range:** on the standard-decimal lane (`CobolDec.ToUnscaled`) a value ≥ 10^38 keeps only its low-order 38 digits, and on the native lane an `Int128` product wraps, so `CONTINUE AFTER 10 ** 40 SECONDS` and `CONTINUE AFTER BIG * BIG SECONDS` (BIG = 2^64) suspend 0 seconds (kb/Work PB1529); every other value above 86,400, including 2^64 and 2^64 + 3, is clamped to 86,400 as stated. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-40 | **COPY statement — rules for identifying and locating default library text**, §7.2.3.3 SR5 and §7.2.3.4 GR3 (with GR2), required + documented | **The default COBOL library is an ordered list of places, searched in GnuCOBOL's order** (CLAUDE.md rule 1: the standard leaves both the list and the search to the implementor): (1) the compiler process's current working directory — the name is first tried as a path relative to it, or as written when it is absolute; (2) each `--copy DIR` in command-line order; (3) with `--nist`, the `copylib` directory beside the source file's directory. The source file's own directory is searched only when it is one of these. The same list serves every COPY in the compilation group, including a COPY inside library text. **Locating a text:** text-name-1 is used as spelled; literal-1's content is a host path (SR5: any non-empty host path is an allowable literal-1 or literal-2). In each place in turn COBOL.NET tries the name as spelled and then with the suffixes `.CPY`, `.CBL`, `.COB`, `.cpy`, `.cbl`, `.cob`, in that order (a name that already contains a period is tried only as spelled), and the FIRST regular file that exists IS the library text; so a text-name names exactly one text in a library (SR3) and no ambiguity is diagnosed. If `BK3.cbl` and `BK3.cob` sit in one directory, `COPY BK3` is `BK3.cbl`. Whether letter case in the name matters is the host file system's rule. **OF/IN library-name-1 or literal-2** names a subdirectory, looked for in each place in the same order, and the text is located in that subdirectory alone. **A library that no place holds, or a text the library does not contain, is the compile-time error CBL3620** (GR2: the library shall be available): compilation fails, and there is no fallback from a named library to the default one and no silent omission of the COPY (GnuCOBOL's fallback to the default library, with a warning, is not followed: GR2 controls). The same at every edition. ⚠ **Not yet what the compiler does:** `Frontend.Preprocess` builds `CopyProcessor` with `strict: false`, so a missing text becomes a comment with no diagnostic, and `FindCopybook` falls back from an unavailable OF/IN library to the default library; and the search order is not yet GnuCOBOL's — the source file's directory is searched first and the working directory is not searched, and every name is tried with `""`, `.cpy`, `.cob`, `.cbl`, `.CPY`, `.COB`, `.CBL` in that order (`CopyProcessor.CopybookExtensions`), so `BK3.cob` beside `BK3.cbl` is taken (kb/Work PB1355). | — |

record.notes: Rule: A.1 item 40 'COPY statement (rules for identifying and locating default library text) ... required ... documented (7.2.3 SR5 and GR3)'. cite.py --check 7.2.3.4 "The implementor shall define the rules for locating the library text referenced by text-name-1 or literal-1" -> OK §7.2.3.4 3) (General rules). cite.py --check 7.2.3.4 "The implementor defines the mechanism for identifying the default COBOL library" -> OK §7.2.3.4 3). cite.py --check 7.2.3.4 "Library-name-1 names a resource that shall be available to the compiler and shall provide access to the library text" -> OK §7.2.3.4 2). cite.py --check 7.2.3.3 "The allowable value of literal-1 and literal-2 is defined by the implementor" -> OK §7.2.3.3 (Syntax rules). cite.py --check 7.2.3.3 "Within one COBOL library, each text-name shall be unique" -> OK §7.2.3.3. Determination: ISO leaves the locating rules and the default-library mechanism to the implementor (GR3) but GR2 is not latitude — an unavailable library or text is a violation, so the row states the error, not today's silent comment/fallback. Suffix ambiguity: PB1355 left 'extension precedence versus ambiguity error' open as implementor latitude; rule-1 precedence to GnuCOBOL (ordered copy-extension list, first hit) keeps the documented precedence, under which each text-name names one text (SR3 satisfied by definition) — no ambiguity diagnostic. Search list read from CompilerDriver.cs:105-114 (--copy paths, NIST copylib appended after) and CopyProcessor.RegisterSourceDir (source dir inserted first). PARTIAL: order + suffix precedence hold (probe BK3 -> CPY); GR2 arms diverge (NOSUCHBOOK silent, P8 OF NOLIB -> DFLT). Owning defect kb/Work PB1355 (open, claims DOC-A.1-40; its 'diagnose an ambiguous text-name' fixer line is superseded by this precedence choice). PB1369's missing-row finding for item 40 is discharged by this row. Witness needed when PB1355 lands: negatives for COPY NOSUCHBOOK and COPY P8 OF NOLIB (CBL3620) at 85 and 2023, and a golden pinning BK3 -> .cpy over .cob. Row stays GAP until then. row: | DOC-A.1-46 | **Data storage — possible representations when the implementation provides multiple ways of storing data**, §8.5.1.1, conditionally required (the condition HOLDS: COBOL.NET stores data in several usages) + documented | **The complete specification is the USAGE clause's: ONE fixed representation per usage, no per-compilation-unit option, each pinned in full by its own row.** **DISPLAY** — one byte per character position (item 209). A position holds a UTF-16 code unit (items 33 and 188); a code unit above U+00FF has no one-byte image, and at EVERY byte channel (a record written to a file, the storage image seen through a REDEFINES or a containing group, CONVERT's BYTE/HEX legs) it is written as `?` (0x3F) **and EC-DATA-CONVERSION is set** — item 33's decided disposition applied to every channel, never a silent substitution. **NATIONAL** — two bytes per position, UTF-16BE (item 213). **BINARY / COMPUTATIONAL / COMP / COMP-4** — big-endian two's complement of the unscaled value in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes by PICTURE digit count (items 205, 208); **COMP-5** has the same representation and owns its full container range (item 208). **BINARY-CHAR / -SHORT / -LONG / -DOUBLE** — 1, 2, 4, 8 bytes, big-endian two's complement (items 206, 207). **PACKED-DECIMAL / COMP-3** — BCD, two digits per byte, trailing sign nibble (item 215; `PIC S9(5) COMP-3` is 3 bytes). **FLOAT-SHORT / COMP-1 / FLOAT-BINARY-32** — IEEE 754 binary32, 4 bytes; **FLOAT-LONG / FLOAT-EXTENDED / COMP-2 / FLOAT-BINARY-64** — IEEE 754 binary64, 8 bytes; big-endian interchange bytes unless an endianness-phrase says otherwise (items 207, 48). **INDEX** — an 8-byte big-endian occurrence number (item 211). **POINTER, FUNCTION-POINTER, PROGRAM-POINTER, OBJECT REFERENCE** — one managed reference, 8 bytes by `FUNCTION BYTE-LENGTH` (items 216, 210, 214; PROGRAM-POINTER is item 217). **BIT** — one bit per boolean position, rounded up to whole bytes (`PIC 1(8) USAGE BIT` is 1 byte, `PIC 1(9)` is 2); a boolean item of usage DISPLAY is one character position per boolean position. Figurative constants: item 74. **Not provided** (refused by name, COBOLNET1564 / COBOLNET1943): FLOAT-BINARY-128 and FLOAT-DECIMAL-16/-34 (§2, Annex A.3 items 17 and 19) and MESSAGE-TAG (A.3 item 4). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-49 | **DEFINE directive — mechanism for providing the value of a compilation-variable-name from the operating environment**, §7.3.11.4 GR4, required + documented | **The compiler process's environment variable whose name is the compilation-variable-name in its canonical UPPER-CASE spelling**, read once, when the `>>DEFINE … AS PARAMETER` directive is processed. A compilation-variable-name is a COBOL word, so every spelling of one name (`MyVar`, `MYVAR`, `myvar`) reads the SAME variable, `MYVAR`, on every host, including a host whose environment names are case-sensitive. **Absent variable ⇒ the name is NOT defined** (GR4's second sentence), and a definition it had before the directive is removed. **Present variable ⇒ the name is defined with the variable's text as its value**: NUMERIC when the whole text parses as an invariant-culture decimal number (surrounding white space, a leading or trailing sign, `.` as the decimal point and `,` as a group separator are accepted — `7`, ` -2.5 `, `1,000`), otherwise ALPHANUMERIC with the text exactly as given (an empty variable is a zero-length alphanumeric value). Every read is recorded on the compilation's inputs (`CompilationInputs.EnvironmentReads`). The same lookup serves the DISPLAY directive's PARAMETER operand (item 55). | — |

record.notes: A.1 item 49 (7.3.11 GR4): required, documented. cite.py --check 7.3.11.4 'is obtained from the operating environment by an implementor-defined method' -> OK §7.3.11.4 4) (General rules). The method is implementor latitude; the row documents the method owning note kb/Work/PB1533 decides ('Normalize the looked-up name (the canonical upper-case COBOL word), document the method (name mapping, typing, absent-variable behaviour)'), because a compilation-variable-name is one case-insensitive COBOL word and a spelling-dependent value source is a wrong answer. DIVERGES: ConditionalCompilationProcessor.ApplyDefine's DefineKind.Parameter arm (pin 80de60472, ~line 484) calls inputs.GetEnvironmentVariable(name) with the name AS SPELLED — no upper-casing — so on a case-sensitive host (Linux) '>>DEFINE MyVar AS PARAMETER' with MYVAR=x is NOT DEFINED (PB1533 repro, adjudicator adj-a1-w1-s2, Linux). Windows probe d2def.cob cannot show it (Windows environment names are case-insensitive): no env -> NOT-DEFINED; MYVAR=x NUMV=7 -> DEFINED + NUMV-GT5; NUMV='1,000' -> NUMV-GT5 (typing = decimal.TryParse NumberStyles.Number, invariant culture — matches the row). Typing and absent-variable arms already hold; only the name mapping diverges. Witness owed: a golden (or unit test over CompilationInputs with an injected environment) defining MyVar AS PARAMETER with only MYVAR set, expecting DEFINED, plus the numeric/alphanumeric typing. Adjacent: PB1367 (SR2 bypass on the PARAMETER arm, different defect).

row: | DOC-A.1-53 | **DISPLAY directive — conversion of data transferred**, §7.3.12.4 GR1 (with GR2, GR4), required + documented | **Each operand is converted to a character image and the images of one directive are written as ONE line to the compiler's standard output, at compile time, during text manipulation.** The compiler produces no source listing (item 117), so GR2 makes the result the implementor's; COBOL.NET follows GnuCOBOL (CLAUDE.md rule 1 precedence), which writes the operands to the compiler's standard output when the directive is processed. Conversion: an **alphanumeric or national literal** transfers its characters without the delimiters and with no other change; a **boolean literal or boolean-expression-1** transfers its value as the boolean characters `0` and `1`; an **arithmetic-expression-1** (a numeric literal included) is evaluated in compile-time arithmetic and transfers its value in the shortest decimal form: a leading `-` only when negative, at least one integer digit, and a `.` followed by the fraction digits only when the value is not an integer, with no trailing zeros (`42`, `-2.5`, `0.125`); a **PARAMETER** operand transfers the environment value's text unchanged (item 55). The images are joined in operand order (GR4) with ONE space between them and the line ends with the host newline — `>>DISPLAY "HELLO-COMPILE" 42` writes `HELLO-COMPILE 42`. With no UPON phrase (GR6's UPON LISTING) the line goes to standard output; UPON compile-time-device-1 is item 54. Nothing is added to the compiled program's own output. | — |

record.notes: A.1 item 53 (7.3.12 GR1): required, documented. cite.py --check 7.3.12.4 'Any conversion of data required is defined by the implementor' -> OK §7.3.12.4 1) (General rules); 7.3.12.4 'If the compiler does not produce a source listing, the result of the DISPLAY directive is defined by the implementor' -> OK §7.3.12.4 2); 7.3.12.4 'the default is as if UPON LISTING were specified' -> OK §7.3.12.4 6); 7.3.12.1 'transfers data to the source listing or an implementor defined compile-time-device' -> OK §7.3.12.1 (General). Latitude settled by rule-1 precedence -> GnuCOBOL 3.2 (cobc/pplex.l display_finish puts() the collected operands to compile-time stdout; testsuite syn_misc.at '>>DISPLAY "OK"' prints OK) — the precedent and disposition already decided in kb/Work/PB1538 ('Transfer the operands to the compiler's standard output'). ISO controls the CONTENT (GR1 'the contents of each operand', GR4 order), so the row evaluates expressions rather than echoing their text; the single-space separator follows PB1538's expected 'HELLO-COMPILE 42'. DIVERGES: probe d2dd.cob (pin 80de60472, --std 2023, XYZ=abc): compile stdout and stderr EMPTY, rc 0; run prints only RUN — the directive is consumed with no transfer (DirectiveStateRegistry 'NONE HELD'). Owning note kb/Work/PB1538 (open; claims DOC-A.1-53/-55); the row text is PB1369's deliverable (PB1369 also claims it). Witness owed: a conformance test capturing the compiler's stdout for >>DISPLAY with literal, arithmetic, boolean operands. Editions: the directive is 2023-only (COBOLNET0900 below).

row: | DOC-A.1-54 | **DISPLAY directive — meaning of compile-time-device-1**, §7.3.12.4 GR5 b), required + documented | **compile-time-device-1 is one of the OUTPUT-capable device-names of the SPECIAL-NAMES table (item 189), naming the same stream in the compiler process:** `CONSOLE` and `SYSOUT` — the compiler's standard output; `SYSERR` — the compiler's standard error. `SYSIN` (input only) and any other word are a compile-time error naming the available devices, from the one `ImplementorNames` table, so the directive and a SPECIAL-NAMES entry can never disagree about what a device-name means. `UPON LISTING` (GR5 a) goes to the device used for source listings; no listing is produced (item 117), so that device is the compiler's standard output, the same place as an omitted UPON phrase (GR6, item 53). An UPON phrase naming several devices, or devices and LISTING (§5.2.6.4 choice indicators, each at most once), writes the line once to each named destination, in the order written. | — |

record.notes: A.1 item 54 (7.3.12 GR5): required, documented. cite.py --check 7.3.12.4 'data is transferred to the device defined by the implementor for receiving that data' -> OK §7.3.12.4 5) (General rules); 7.3.12.4 'the default is as if UPON LISTING were specified' -> OK §7.3.12.4 6). No precedent: GnuCOBOL 3.2's >>DISPLAY has no UPON device (its lexer collects the words as text, per doc-rows-1's reading of cobc/pplex.l); IBM Enterprise COBOL and Micro Focus have no ISO DISPLAY directive. The determination therefore reuses the implementation's own device-name table (DOC-A.1-189: CONSOLE/SYSOUT = stdout, SYSERR = stderr, SYSIN input-only) — one rule written in one place — and diagnoses any other word, which is the fix kb/Work/PB807 owes (its title: 'ANY operand is then accepted'; its A.1-54 paragraph: 'accepts any word although the implementation defines no device'). The choice has no significant consequence beyond which stream receives a compile-time message, so it is not an owner question. DIVERGES: probe d2dd.cob (pin 80de60472 --std 2023): '>>DISPLAY "DEV" UPON NOSUCHDEVICE' and '>>DISPLAY "ERR" UPON SYSERR' both compile clean (rc 0), nothing on compiler stdout or stderr — no device is defined, any word is accepted, nothing is transferred. Owning note kb/Work/PB807 (open; operand/UPON syntax and the undiagnosed device name); the transfer itself is kb/Work/PB1538; the row text is PB1369's deliverable. Witness owed: a negative golden for an undefined device name and a stderr-capturing test for UPON SYSERR.

row: | DOC-A.1-55 | **DISPLAY directive — mechanism for providing the value of a compilation-variable-name from the operating environment**, §7.3.12.4 GR3, required + documented | **The same mechanism as the DEFINE directive's PARAMETER phrase (item 49): the compiler process's environment variable whose name is the compilation-variable-name in its canonical UPPER-CASE spelling**, read when the DISPLAY directive is processed, so `PARAMETER MyVar` and `PARAMETER MYVAR` read the same variable on every host. A present variable's text is transferred unchanged, with no numeric conversion (item 53); an empty variable transfers an empty image. **When the variable is absent, that DISPLAY directive transfers nothing at all** — no line is written for any of its operands (GR3: "no transfer shall take place"). The name is not thereby defined as a compilation variable; only a DEFINE directive defines one. | — |

record.notes: A.1 item 55 (7.3.12 GR3): required, documented. cite.py --check 7.3.12.4 'If no value is made available from the operating environment no transfer shall take place' -> OK §7.3.12.4 3) (General rules). The method is implementor latitude; GnuCOBOL 3.2 has no PARAMETER form for >>DISPLAY (doc-rows-1: '>>DISPLAY PARAMETER XYZ' prints 'PARAMETER XYZ'), so the precedence gives no answer and kb/Work/PB1538's 'To close' decides it: 'decide the PARAMETER lookup with kb/Work PB1533 (the >>DEFINE PARAMETER environment lookup)' — one lookup for both directives, documented as DOC-A.1-49 (upper-cased name, PB1533's fix). The absent-variable arm reads GR3's 'no transfer shall take place' as the whole directive (the literal reading: GR3 names the transfer, not the operand). DIVERGES: probe d2dd.cob (pin 80de60472 --std 2023, XYZ=abc): '>>DISPLAY PARAMETER XYZ' compiles clean and writes nothing — the environment is never consulted and the directive never transfers (the no-value/no-transfer half holds only vacuously). row: | DOC-A.1-68 | **Externalized names — formation and mapping rules**, §7.3.9.3 GR2 a) and b), §8.3.2.2, required + documented | **Formation.** An externalized name is a string of characters. For a name written as a COBOL word with no AS phrase (a program-name, a user-function-name, a class-name, an interface-name, an EXTERNAL data-name or file-name) it is the word's spelling. For a name given by an `AS literal` it is the literal's content with **leading and trailing spaces removed**; spaces inside the name are kept. A CALL, CANCEL or `ADDRESS OF PROGRAM` target is formed the same way: a literal's content, or an identifier's content, with leading and trailing spaces removed. ISO leaves formation to the implementor (§8.3.2.2). GnuCOBOL removes leading and trailing spaces, with a warning, from a CALL or CANCEL literal and from a literal program-name, but keeps an AS literal as written, so a GnuCOBOL program named `AS "trail  "` cannot be called. COBOL.NET removes them from AS names too, so that every externalized name is formed by one rule, and gives a compile-time warning when an AS literal has leading or trailing spaces. **Mapping.** Two externalized names are the same name when they are equal ignoring case: `CALL "sub-p"` and `CALL "SUB-P"` both reach `PROGRAM-ID. SUB-P`, and `EXTERNAL AS "Shared Two"` and `EXTERNAL AS "shared two"` are one data item. A program with an AS phrase is reached by its AS name, never by its declared word. **CALL-CONVENTION (§7.3.9).** COBOL.NET defines no call-convention-name. `>>CALL-CONVENTION COBOL` (the default, §7.3.9.3 GR1) is the only accepted form, so GR2 a) always applies: program-names and method-names in CALL, CANCEL, INVOKE and program-address-identifiers map by the COBOL-word rule above. `>>CALL-CONVENTION` followed by any other word is a compile-time error, because that word names no convention and therefore no GR2 b) literal mapping. ⚠ Two parts are not yet implemented: an AS name with leading or trailing spaces is stored with the spaces, so `PROGRAM-ID. S AS "trail  "` cannot be reached even by `CALL "trail  "`, and an EXTERNAL `AS "Shared Two "` does not share with `AS "shared two"`, and no warning is given (kb/Work PB1539); and `>>CALL-CONVENTION XYZZY` is accepted without a diagnostic (kb/Work PB1383). | `conformance:2002/pb303_as_externalized_name` |

row: | DOC-A.1-75 | **File sharing — interaction with other facilities and languages**, §9.1.15, optional (documented if provided) | **Provided: other facilities see COBOL file sharing only as a host lock on the physical file.** When an OPEN succeeds, the connector takes a host lock on the physical file chosen from BOTH its sharing mode (§9.1.15 rules 1–3) and its open mode, so that another opener — in this run unit, in another COBOL.NET run unit, or in another language that honours the lock — is admitted or refused exactly as §9.1.15 Table 19 decides. A connector with no sharing mode specified locks as the implementor-default mode (item 77). The lock lasts until the connector is closed. The reverse direction also holds: when the host refuses a COBOL.NET OPEN because another process, in any language, holds the file under an incompatible lock or share mode, the OPEN fails with I-O status **61** (§9.1.13.9 1)); a DELETE FILE refused the same way gets **62**. **On Windows** the lock is the host share mode, and every process on the machine is bound by it. **On Linux and macOS** the lock is an advisory POSIX record lock (`fcntl`), taken according to both the connector's sharing mode and its open mode, so every COBOL.NET run unit is arbitrated by §9.1.15 Table 19; a program in another language is bound only if it takes `fcntl` locks the same way. A program that opens the file without locking is neither stopped nor detected. ⚠ Not yet implemented on Linux and macOS: the runtime expresses READ ONLY (and the clause-less default) through .NET `FileShare.Read`, which .NET implements as a shared `flock`, and a shared `flock` does not refuse a writer. So while a READ ONLY connector has the file open, another run unit's `OPEN EXTEND` or `OPEN I-O` still succeeds with 00; and a whole-file two-state lock keyed on the sharing mode alone cannot express Table 19 at all (it cannot admit concurrent `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` writers while refusing a `READ ONLY` connector's writer), so the lock layout is kb/Work PB833's design (kb/Work PB833). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-77 | **File sharing — the default sharing mode when none is specified**, §9.1.15, §14.9.27.4 GR23 (and §9.1.3), required + documented | **It depends on the open mode.** When neither the OPEN statement's SHARING phrase nor the file control entry's SHARING clause gives a mode, the OPEN establishes one of §9.1.15's own modes for the connector: **`OPEN INPUT` opens `SHARING WITH READ ONLY`**, and **`OPEN OUTPUT`, `OPEN I-O` and `OPEN EXTEND` open `SHARING WITH NO OTHER`**. The mode lasts until the connector is closed, and every other connector is arbitrated against it by §9.1.15 Table 19, whether that connector is in this run unit or in another one. So with two clause-less connectors on one file: `OPEN INPUT` and a second `OPEN INPUT` both succeed with 00; `OPEN INPUT` followed by a second connector's `OPEN I-O`, `OPEN EXTEND` or `OPEN OUTPUT` fails with 61; and any OPEN of a file that a clause-less connector holds open in OUTPUT, I-O or EXTEND mode fails with 61. The host lock for these modes is described in item 75. This follows GnuCOBOL, which locks a file shared for input and exclusive for every other mode; ISO leaves the choice to the implementor (CLAUDE.md rule 1). This row covers COBOL 2002, 2014 and 2023. The COBOL-85 behaviour, where the 6x statuses do not exist, is kb/Work PB670. ⚠ Not yet implemented: the runtime establishes no mode for a clause-less connector (`FileRegistry.ImplementorDefaultSharing` is `null`) and reports a conflict only where every candidate mode would, so today both `OPEN OUTPUT` followed by another connector's `OPEN INPUT`, and `OPEN INPUT` followed by another connector's `OPEN I-O`, answer 00 (kb/Work PB322 determination A). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-81 | **Floating-point numeric item — alignment when used as a receiving operand**, §14.6.8.3 rule 1, required — documentation NOT required by A.1 (VOLUNTARY) | **One correctly rounded conversion to the receiver's own format.** The sending operand's algebraic value (for a decimal sender, every digit it holds) is converted in ONE step to the nearest value the receiver can represent. Ties go to even, ISO/IEC 60559 round-to-nearest. `FLOAT-SHORT` and `COMP-1` hold IEEE binary32. `FLOAT-LONG`, `FLOAT-EXTENDED` and `COMP-2` hold binary64 (item 207). `FLOAT-BINARY-32`/`-64` convert the same way, as §14.6.8.3 rule 2 requires. The value is never rounded first to a wider binary format and then narrowed. A value too small for the normal range becomes the nearest subnormal, or zero when it is closer to zero than half the smallest subnormal. A value too large for the format is the §14.9.25.4 GR6 d)4.a case covered in §3 ("EC-DATA-NOT-FINITE / EC-DATA-OVERFLOW applied to EVERY floating-point usage"): with checking off the result is ±Infinity, and with EC-DATA-OVERFLOW checking on the exception condition is raised. So `MOVE 0.1 TO` a FLOAT-SHORT stores 0.100000001490116…, and `MOVE 1.000000059604644775390625000001 TO` a FLOAT-SHORT stores 1.00000011920928955 (the binary32 neighbour nearer the value), not 1. ⚠ Not yet implemented for binary32 receivers: a sender whose usage differs from the receiver's is converted to binary64 first and then cast to binary32, so it is rounded twice, and the second example stores 1 (kb/Work PB1110). row: | DOC-A.1-89 | **Function-identifier — the runtime resources checked before a user-defined function is executed**, §8.4.3.2.4 GR6 c), required + documented | **The set of runtime resources checked is EMPTY, so a function activation never raises EC-PROGRAM-RESOURCES** — the determination item 14 makes for CALL, applied to a user-defined function. COBOL.NET checks no runtime resource beyond locating the function (GR6 b): a function is located when its externalized name (item 68) matches a function registered in the run unit — compiled into the calling assembly, or a separately compiled module `<name>.dll` beside the application whose `__CobolModule.Register()` registrar has run (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule`, the lookup CALL uses). A module file that exists but cannot be loaded (a truncated or foreign image, or a dependency the registrar itself needs) or whose registrar throws has therefore NOT been located: **EC-FUNCTION-NOT-FOUND** is set, the function activation is not successful, and execution continues as GR6 f) specifies. **Available memory and activation depth are not checked**: running out of either is a host failure, the run unit ends abnormally and no exception condition is set. row: | DOC-A.1-102 | **INVOKE statement — the runtime resources checked before a method is executed**, §14.9.23.4 GR7 b) — Annex A.1 cites GR7 e), but the resource sentence is GR7 b); required + documented | **One resource is checked: that the class which provides the method can be loaded and initialized.** When §9.3.6 resolution finds the method, the INVOKE checks that the class's assembly and its dependencies can be loaded, and that the class's type initialization, including the allocation of its factory storage on first use, completes. If either fails, **EC-OO-METHOD** is set, the method invocation fails, and execution continues as GR7 g) specifies. The standard gives this outcome to both "method not found" and "resources not available". Today every class a program can INVOKE is compiled into its own compilation group's assembly, which is already loaded, so only initialization can fail. The load check applies to classes that come from a referenced repository assembly (item 67, kb/Work R44). **Available memory and activation depth are not checked.** Running out of either is a host failure: the run unit ends abnormally and no exception condition is set. The CALL twin (item 14) and the function twin (item 89) count a module that cannot be loaded as NOT LOCATED rather than as a resource failure; for INVOKE the distinction has no observable effect, because GR7 b) gives both outcomes EC-OO-METHOD. ⚠ Not yet implemented: EC-OO-METHOD is raised only when no class in the hierarchy declares the method (`CobolObject.__CobolInvoke`). A failure to load or initialize the class escapes as a .NET exception instead (kb/Work PB1422). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-103 | **I-O status — the action taken for a fatal exception condition**, §9.1.13.1 (with §14.6.13.1.3 rule 3), required + documented | **Continue only when the program is equipped to see the failure; otherwise terminate.** The fatal I-O statuses are those that begin with 3, 4 or 7, and every 9x status COBOL.NET defines (item 110). The action is decided after the I-O status is stored and any applicable USE procedure has run. **With checking for the EC-I-O condition not enabled (the default):** execution **continues** if the file connector has a FILE STATUS clause or a USE procedure applied to the statement. Control passes to the end of the statement that produced the status, and its NOT AT END or NOT INVALID KEY phrase is not executed (§9.1.13.1). If the connector has **neither**, the run unit **terminates abnormally** (§14.6.12): the message names the file, the statement and the I-O status, and the exit code is nonzero (§2 row 44). **With checking enabled** (`>>TURN EC-I-O CHECKING ON`, or a level above it), COBOL.NET adds nothing: §14.6.13.1.3 rules 4–7 apply after the I-O rules. A PERFORM WHEN phrase or a RESUME in the declarative can continue execution; otherwise the run unit terminates abnormally, even when the file has a FILE STATUS clause. This follows GnuCOBOL, which ends the run unit on a fatal status only when no declarative applies and the file has no FILE STATUS clause; ISO leaves the choice to the implementor (CLAUDE.md rule 1). A host failure inside a READ or WRITE is reported as status 30 and handled by this rule the same way. ⚠ Not yet implemented: in a default build, a file with neither a FILE STATUS clause nor a USE procedure **continues** after a fatal status (`OPEN INPUT` of a missing file answers 35, and the next statement runs with exit code 0; kb/Work PB322 E). A host `IOException` inside a sequential READ or WRITE escapes as an unhandled .NET exception instead of status 30 (kb/Work PB1512). The continue and checking-enabled arms already behave as stated. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-105 | **I-O status, permanent error — the technique for correcting it**, §9.1.13.1, optional + documented if provided | **Provided: the technique is CLOSE.** A permanent error condition (an I-O status beginning with '3', §9.1.13.6) belongs to the file connector that got it, and it stays in effect until that connector is closed. **After a failed OPEN** ('30', '31', '35', '37', '38' — COBOL-85 to 2014 only: CLOSE WITH LOCK and status '38' were removed at 2023 — or '39') the connector is left closed. That closed state is already the corrected state, so the next OPEN of the file starts fresh. **After a failed READ, WRITE, REWRITE, DELETE or START** on an open connector ('30' or '34'), the condition stays in effect. Every later input-output statement on that connector, except CLOSE, is unsuccessful. It does not touch the physical file, it sets the same I-O status again, and it raises that status's exception condition again (§9.1.13.1). A CLOSE runs normally, and its success ends the condition, so the next OPEN starts clean. This applies to every organization and every edition. Example: a random relative WRITE with relative key 0 answers '34' (§14.9.51.4 GR29 b). The next WRITE, with key 1, also answers '34' and writes nothing. CLOSE answers '00', and after OPEN I-O the WRITE with key 1 answers '00'. | — |

record.notes: Rule: A.1 105 is optional + documented if provided. cite.py --check 9.1.13.1 "unless an implementor-defined technique is invoked to correct the permanent error condition" -> OK §9.1.13.1 (General). The persistence sentence is NORMATIVE (ISO controls, so rule-1 precedence does not reach it). Only the correction technique is latitude. GnuCOBOL 3.x keeps no permanent-error state and retries every statement, so it offers no precedent for the technique. The technique chosen here, CLOSE, is the one kb/Work PB1541 names as the natural one. It also matches the IBM/Micro Focus guidance that a file with a 3x status must be closed. 'Not provided' cannot be written: the condition would then outlive CLOSE and re-OPEN, which no implementation does and which §9.1.13.6 5) makes absurd (a '35' file created later could never be opened). Probe scratchpad/doc2/out/run/d4/p105.cob (--std 2023, pin 80de60472): OPEN 00 / WRITE key 0 -> 34 (neither INVALID KEY arm runs) / WRITE key 1 -> 00 (NIK) / CLOSE 00 / OPEN INPUT of a missing file 35 / READ 47. The second WRITE should be '34' with nothing written, so this DIVERGES. The defect is still open: kb/Work PB1541 (open) owns it. PB1534 currently lists the row, and PB1541 should claim it. Sibling: PB1192 decides whether key 0 stays '34' (DOC-A.1-107 keeps it '34' per GR29 b)). Witness needed: a golden that gets a '3x' on an open connector and shows the next statement repeats it, then CLOSE plus re-OPEN clears it.

row: | DOC-A.1-107 | **I-O status 24 — the manner in which the boundaries of a relative or indexed file are defined**, §9.1.13.5 item 4 + §14.9.51.4 GR33 b) / GR42 d), required + documented | **The boundary of a physical relative or indexed file is its storage capacity.** A WRITE is outside the boundary when the file cannot grow to hold the record. That happens when the host medium is full, when a host quota or file-size limit is reached (POSIX ENOSPC / EDQUOT / EFBIG; Windows ERROR_DISK_FULL / ERROR_HANDLE_DISK_FULL), or when the file would exceed the largest store the COBOL.NET relative/indexed format can address. That format limit is 2 147 483 647 bytes for the framed store image (`RecordFraming`), counting the 4-byte empty-slot tag of every relative record number below the highest one written. The test runs **at the WRITE**. The WRITE is unsuccessful with I-O status '24', the invalid key condition exists (so the INVALID KEY phrase runs), no record is released, and the file is unchanged. A WRITE is never reported '00' and then failed at CLOSE. **This is separate from the relative key's own range.** A random or dynamic relative WRITE whose relative key is less than 1, or greater than 2 147 483 647 (the highest relative record number permitted for the file), answers '34' as §14.9.51.4 GR29 b) states, and takes no INVALID KEY branch. GR29 b) names that case explicitly, so it governs over the general GR33 b); GnuCOBOL's '24' for key 0 is not followed because the standard decides it. On a sequential-access WRITE, a relative record number with more significant digits than the relative key answers '24' (§14.9.51.4 GR29 a), §9.1.13.5 item 4); in random or dynamic access the record number comes from the key, so it cannot happen. Same in every edition. | — |

The manner of defining the boundary is latitude. This row uses storage capacity, which matches GnuCOBOL 3.x (libcob/fileio.c errno_cob_sts: ENOSPC/EDQUOT map to a boundary violation) and IBM (out of space is a boundary violation). The key<1 contradiction that kb/Work PB1192 flags for the owner is settled by ISO itself: GR29 b) is the explicit, specific sentence for the relative key value ('less than 1 or greater than the highest relative record number permitted for the file' -> '34'). GR33 b) covers the storage boundary ('24'), so the two concepts are distinct and both hold. GnuCOBOL answers '24' for key 0 (relative_write, kindex < 0), but the ISO-first precedence of CLAUDE.md rule 1 does not reach GnuCOBOL. Code at pin 80de60472: key 0 -> '34' (scratchpad/doc2/out/run/d4/p105.cob, W0 34, no INVALID KEY arm), which matches the row. There is no capacity test: per PB1192, RRN 5000000 -> '00' plus a 20 MB store, a store past Int32 fails at CLOSE, and IndexedConnector.Write has no '24' arm. So this DIVERGES, owned by kb/Work PB1192 (open, inventory_rows include DOC-A.1-107). The 2 147 483 647 limits are the current store format's own ceiling ((int)composed.Length in WriteStore). If PB1192 re-architects the store (rule 5), it restates the number in this row in the same change set.

row: | DOC-A.1-108 | **I-O status 34 — the manner in which the boundaries of a sequential file are defined**, §9.1.13.6 item 3 + §14.9.51.4 GR20, required + documented | **The boundary of a physical sequential file (record sequential or line sequential) is the capacity of the host medium.** A WRITE is outside the boundary when the host cannot store the record because the medium is full or a host quota or file-size limit is reached (POSIX ENOSPC / EDQUOT / EFBIG; Windows ERROR_DISK_FULL / ERROR_HANDLE_DISK_FULL). The failure is detected at the WRITE, including a buffered write that fails when the host flushes it. The WRITE is unsuccessful with I-O status '34', a permanent error (EC-I-O-PERMANENT-ERROR). No part of the record counts as written, and the file stays open. Under item 105 the condition then stays in effect on that connector until it is closed. Any other host failure during a WRITE is '30' (§9.1.13.6 item 1), never an escaped .NET exception. No other sequential boundary exists: there is no record-count or size limit below the medium's. Same in every edition. | — |

record.notes: cite.py --check 9.1.13.6 "an attempt is made to write outside the externally-defined boundaries of a physical sequential file" -> OK §9.1.13.6 3). Both agree with this row. row: | DOC-A.1-113 | **Life cycle for objects — timing and algorithm for deciding that an object can no longer take part in continued execution**, §9.3.14.3, required (A.1 does not require it to be documented; documented here because it decides when §9.1.4's implicit CLOSE of an object's files happens) | **Reachability, decided by the .NET garbage collector.** An instance object is a managed instance of a class derived from `CobolObject`. It can no longer take part in continued execution once no object reference in the run unit reaches it. The .NET tracing garbage collector decides that at a time of its own choosing, which is nondeterministic, as §9.3.14.3 permits. When it has decided, the object is destroyed. Its finalizer implicitly CLOSEs every per-object file connector the object owns (§9.1.4, 'when the object is deleted'), **in the run unit that created the object**, and the object's storage is reclaimed. A later OPEN of the same physical file is therefore arbitrated only against connectors that are still live. At run-unit termination every object not yet destroyed is destroyed, and its files are closed with the run unit's (`CobolFile.CloseAll`). Whichever of the two happens first is the destruction. An object that owns no file has no observable destruction beyond its storage being reclaimed. COBOL 2002 and later. | — |

The timing is latitude, and GC reachability is the §9.3.14.3 NOTE's own garbage-collection model. GnuCOBOL has no OO runtime, so it offers no precedent; the choice is the .NET platform's. row: | DOC-A.1-114 | **Line delimiter — specification of**, §12.4.5.10.3 GR2 (+ §9.1.13.2 item 5's '06'), required + documented | **The line delimiter is the host platform's newline:** CR LF (U+000D U+000A) on Windows and LF (U+000A) on Linux and macOS (`Environment.NewLine`). **WRITE** ends every record with that delimiter, and ADVANCING and LINAGE positioning add their own line and page controls around it. **READ** ends a record at an LF, or at a CR LF pair on any host, so a file written on either platform reads back on the other. A final line with no delimiter ends at end of file. **A lone CR (one not followed by LF) is not a delimiter.** It is record data, and because CR is outside the line sequential character set (item 115), the READ that delivers it answers '09'. A line longer than the record area is delivered truncated with '06' (§9.1.13.2), and the rest of the line is the next record. COBOL 2023 (ORGANIZATION LINE SEQUENTIAL). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-124 | **Native arithmetic — when an operand represents an integer**, §5.5 3) a), required + documented | **An operand represents an integer exactly when its value has no nonzero digit to the right of the decimal point.** The test uses the operand's own exact value, never a rounded or truncated copy. A fixed-point data item is tested at its full declared scale. An arithmetic expression is tested on the value the native intermediate data item (item 123) holds for it. A floating-point operand is an integer only when its binary value is exactly integral: COMP-2 `2.0` is an integer, `2 + 1.0E-10` is not. The same value gets the same answer at every rule that asks: a subscript, a reference-modification start or length, a SET index or amount, and an integer argument of an intrinsic function. When checking for the rule's exception condition is enabled, a non-integer is refused by that condition (for example EC-BOUND-SUBSCRIPT). row: | DOC-A.1-131 | **OPEN statement with no SHARING phrase and no SHARING clause — the sharing mode established for the file connector**, §14.9.27.4 GR23 (+ §9.1.15), required + documented | **The default sharing mode depends on the open mode.** OPEN INPUT establishes **SHARING WITH READ ONLY**. OPEN OUTPUT, OPEN I-O and OPEN EXTEND establish **SHARING WITH NO OTHER**. Both are the standard's own modes, so §9.1.15's rules and Table 19 apply to them unchanged. Clause-less readers can share a file. A clause-less updater or writer has the file to itself: its OPEN is refused with '61' while any other connector has the file open, and while it is open every other connector's OPEN is refused with '61'. A clause-less OPEN INPUT is refused with '61' while another connector has the file open in a mode other than input. The same default applies to a file control entry that has a LOCK MODE clause but no SHARING clause, and to an OPEN whose only sharing-related phrase is RETRY. Record locking for such a connector is item 153. Example (three clause-less SELECTs on one file): A OPEN INPUT '00', B OPEN INPUT '00', C OPEN I-O '61', C OPEN EXTEND '61', C OPEN OUTPUT '61'. After A and B close: A OPEN I-O '00', B OPEN INPUT '61', C OPEN I-O '61'. COBOL 2002 and later (the COBOL-85 posture is kb/Work PB670). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-146 | **RECORD clause — the calculations to derive the size of records on the storage medium**, §13.18.43.4 GR2, required + documented | **Start from the record size in bytes (GR1/GR3/GR8)**: every alphanumeric, alphabetic, numeric-display or edited character position is ONE byte (item 209: ISO/IEC 8859-1, owner decision kb/Work R47 — a record holding a character above U+00FF is refused, item 31), a national character position TWO bytes (UTF-16BE, D-N1), and a binary, packed or floating item its item-205–215 width; the implicit or explicit RECORD clause then fixes the size (implicit clause: item 147; format 3: item 148). **Then add the control information of the file's organization:** **(a) record sequential, fixed-length records** (format 1, explicit or implied) — **exactly integer-1 bytes per record, no control information**: a record description shorter than integer-1 is written followed by the rest of the integer-1-byte record area, so the file is `n × integer-1` bytes (`FD F RECORD CONTAINS 20 CHARACTERS` + `01 R PIC X(10)` → 20 bytes per record; an implied format 1 over `01 A PIC X(5)` and `01 B PIC X(10)` → 10 bytes per record, whichever is written); **(b) record sequential, variable-length records** (format 2, format 3, or an implied format 2) — **4 + the record's own byte size**: a 4-byte little-endian length word before each record (item 151), plus `4 + 8 × k` bytes when the record is a variable-length group with k variable components (its extent table, D-FRA (v)); **(c) line sequential** — the record's characters less the trailing spaces §14.9.51.4 GR21 does not transfer (a file whose RECORD clause has the DEPENDING phrase is filled to data-name-1's length instead, GR22), one byte each, plus the line delimiter of item 114 (CR LF on Windows, LF on Linux and macOS); a record area holding a character outside the line sequential character set is not written at all ('71', item 115); **(d) relative and indexed** — the file begins with the store header (20 bytes plus each key's descriptor: the §9.1.6 fixed file attributes, item 129) and EVERY record, fixed-length or variable, is framed as in (b); an empty relative slot is the 4-byte tag `0xFFFFFFFF` alone. **CODE-SET** never changes a size: every claimed code set (the identity sets, and EBCDIC = CCSID 37) is one byte per alphanumeric character, and the framing in (b)–(d) stays native (A.3 item 27). The **FORMAT clause** cannot arise: A.4.8 is not claimed and a FORMAT clause is refused with COBOLNET1705 (A.1 items 84 and 85 cannot arise). ⚠ kb/Work PB1276: arm (a) with an explicit `RECORD CONTAINS integer-1` larger than the largest record description writes the description's size today (10 bytes, not 20); and arm (c)'s delimiter is CR LF on every host today (kb/Work PB1540). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-147 | **RECORD clause — the implicit RECORD clause when no RECORD clause is specified**, §13.18.43.4 GR5, required + documented | **One rule for every file description entry, FD and SD alike** (§3 D-FRA (iv)). **(a) Implied format 2** when any record description of the entry is VARIABLE-LENGTH — a dynamic-length elementary item or a variable-length group (§8.5.1.12.1; `FileModel.IsVariableLengthRecord`): integer-2 is the smallest record description's byte size with every dynamic-length item at zero length, integer-3 the largest with each at its maximum size (GR5 b / GR8 b), and no DEPENDING phrase. **(b) Implied format 1 otherwise**: integer-1 is the byte size of the LARGEST record description entry (GR5 a), an OCCURS DEPENDING ON table counted at its maximum (GR3), so every record of the file is integer-1 bytes — a WRITE, REWRITE or RELEASE of a shorter record description sends the whole integer-1-byte record area, and an ODO record is always sent at its maximum. row: | DOC-A.1-156 | **Reference format — the control characters that terminate a free-form line, and whether they may appear in comments and literals**, §6.1 3) b), required + documented | **Exactly one terminator: LINE FEED (U+000A).** A CARRIAGE RETURN (U+000D) immediately before a LINE FEED is part of that terminator and is not a character of the line, so LF and CR LF files read identically. **No other control character terminates a free-form line** — not a lone CR, not FORM FEED, VERTICAL TAB, NEL or any other C0/C1 control — and ONE set serves every stage that asks where a line ends: the reference-format and compiler-directive stage (`ReferenceFormatProcessor.NormalizeToFreeFormMapped`, where `>>` must begin a line), the floating-comment indicator `*>` (whose comment runs to the end of the line), and literal scanning. The end of the source text also ends its last line. **In comments and literals:** the terminator cannot appear in a comment or in the content of an alphanumeric or national literal — it ends the line (a literal that must span lines ends the first line with the floating literal continuation indicator, §6.2.3.1) — while every other control character, a lone CR included, MAY appear in comment-text and in literal content and is taken as that character: `DISPLAY "A<TAB>B"`, `"A<FF>B"` and `"A<CR>B"` each display three characters. Free-form reference format exists from COBOL-2002 (`>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE`, and the auto-detection of DOC-A.1-158). This is GnuCOBOL's line model (rule 1 precedence; the standard leaves the set to the implementor). ⚠ kb/Work PB1496: the lexer today ends a floating comment AND a literal at a lone CR (`CobolLexer.g4` COMMENT_TEXT / STR_BODY exclude `\r`), while the directive stage does not, so `DISPLAY "A"<CR>>>DEFINE X AS 1` is COBOL0307 and `"A<CR>B"` is an unterminated literal. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-157 | **Reference format — the meaning of lines and character positions, free-form and fixed-form**, §6.1 1) c), required + documented | **A character position is ONE UTF-16 code unit of the decoded source text** (each file decoded by its byte-order mark, UTF-8 without one, ISO/IEC 8859-1 when it is not well-formed UTF-8 — DOC-A.1-25, DOC-A.1-26): a character of the Basic Multilingual Plane is one position and a character outside it is two, EXCEPT a horizontal tab (U+0009), which advances to the next tab stop — positions 1, 9, 17, 25, … (a tab width of 8, GnuCOBOL's default `tab-width`; rule 1 precedence) — so it occupies one to eight positions. **A line is the text of a source or library file between two line terminators** (DOC-A.1-156: LF, or CR LF), the terminator not included; the file's end also ends its last line. There is no record or block structure below the file. **Free-form:** a line has 0 to **255** character positions (§6.1 3) a)); a longer line is diagnosed, and program text may begin at any position. **Fixed-form:** positions 1–6 are the sequence number area, position 7 the indicator area and positions 8–72 the program-text area; margin R follows position 72 and anything beyond it is ignored (DOC-A.1-158). **A line shorter than 72 positions is read as if space-filled to margin R**, so its program-text area is always the 65 positions 8–72 — which is what an alphanumeric or boolean literal continued by the fixed continuation indicator carries to its continuation (§6.3.5: “any spaces at the end of the fixed-form continued line are part of the literal”), e.g. `000100 01 X PIC X(80) VALUE "AB` ending at position 29, continued by `000100-    "CD".`, gives `AB` + 43 spaces + `CD`. Fixed-form is available at every edition, free-form from COBOL-2002. This follows GnuCOBOL and IBM Enterprise COBOL, which both pad a short record to the margin (rule 1 precedence). ⚠ Three edges diverge today: a short fixed-form line is NOT padded, so the example gives `ABCD` (kb/Work PB1491); a free-form line over 255 positions is accepted silently (kb/Work PB1496); and a TAB counts as one position, so a fixed-form line beginning with two TABs is misread (kb/Work PB1586). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-167 | **Run unit — the relationship and interaction between COBOL and non-COBOL components**, §14.6.1, conditionally required (condition met: a .NET host can activate COBOL.NET programs, items 65, 141) + documented | **The only non-COBOL component a run unit can contain is .NET code that ACTIVATES COBOL.NET programs** (a "host"); COBOL never activates non-COBOL code — a CALL cannot reach it (item 16) and CANCEL does not touch it (item 19). **Beginning:** an executable built by `cobol` begins its run unit in its generated `Main` and contains no host. A host begins a run unit with `RunUnit.Run(body)`, which gives it a FRESH run unit — program table, EXTERNAL items, files, switches, locale (read from the process once, at that moment — item 120), FUNCTION RANDOM sequence, report state and exception status — then calls each compiled module's `__CobolModule.Register()` and activates programs by name (`ProgramRegistry.CallProgram`, item 65) or through `ICobolProgram.Call` (item 141). An activation outside `RunUnit.Run` joins the ambient run unit of the host's execution context (`RunUnit.Current`, one per async flow). **Storage:** the host and COBOL share only what an activation passes — the USING arguments and the RETURNING item (item 141); COBOL storage is otherwise invisible to the host, and each run unit's EXTERNAL items are its own. **Ending normally:** GOBACK or EXIT PROGRAM returns to the host at its call site (item 65); the run unit ends when `RunUnit.Run`'s body returns, or at process exit for the ambient run unit, and either way the §14.6.11 actions run (every open file of the run unit closed). **STOP RUN, and a fatal exception condition that terminates the run unit (§14.6.12), end the RUN UNIT ONLY — never the host process** (owner decision kb/Work R48, deliberately unlike GnuCOBOL's process exit): COBOL.NET performs the §14.6.11 actions (every file of the run unit closed), resets the run unit's state (switches, SET LOCALE — item 168 —, report and exception state), and returns control to the host as ONE documented, catchable .NET exception type carrying the exit status (the item-192 STOP RUN status, or the abnormal-termination status) and whether termination was normal or abnormal; no other exception type escapes to the host for a run-unit ending, and `Environment.Exit` is never called. The host process continues and may begin another run unit, which inherits nothing. A standalone `cobol` executable IS its own host: its `Main` catches that ending and exits the process with the status. Every edition. ⚠ Diverges today: STOP RUN throws the internal `StopRun` signal into the host (out of `RunUnit.Run` too); a fatal EC reaches the abnormal-termination surface only on the `RunMain` path; files are not closed for the ambient run unit (kb/Work PB1149, PB1253); and switch, locale and report state carry over into the next run unit (kb/Work PB1069). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-192 | **STOP and GOBACK statements — constraints on the value of the STATUS literal or on the contents of the data item referenced by the STATUS identifier**, §14.9.42.4 GR5 · §14.9.18.4 GR10, required + documented | **No value is refused; the STATUS operand becomes the process exit code** (`Environment.ExitCode`, the one observable .NET gives both the value GR5 passes and the ERROR/NORMAL indication of GR2/GR3). The syntax rules still apply (§14.9.42.3 SR2–SR4: an integer data item or a display/national item; a numeric literal-1 an integer; no zero-length literal; `STATUS NULL` is COBOLNET1704). The mapping, shared by STOP and a main program's GOBACK (DOC-A.1-94): **(1)** a numeric operand's integer value (a data item's value truncated toward zero) is the exit code; **(2)** a non-numeric operand — an alphanumeric or national item, a non-numeric, national, hexadecimal or boolean literal, a figurative constant, `ALL literal` — is decoded as an unsigned integer from its digit characters, a non-digit position adding no digit (`CobolNum.FromAlphanumeric`), so `STATUS "007"` exits 7 and `STATUS "ABEND"` or `STATUS SPACE` exits 0; **(3)** the host keeps what it can report: the value is CLAMPED (never wrapped) to the 32-bit range, so `STATUS 4294967296` exits 2,147,483,647, and a POSIX host keeps only the low 8 bits, so `STATUS 300` exits 44 and `STATUS -3` exits 253. **A STATUS value, when present, wins over ERROR or NORMAL** — `STOP RUN WITH ERROR STATUS 0` exits 0 and `WITH NORMAL STATUS 7` exits 7; with no STATUS value `WITH ERROR` exits 1 and `WITH NORMAL` (or no phrase) exits 0. row: | DOC-A.1-214 | **USAGE OBJECT REFERENCE clause — amount of storage allocated**, §13.18.60.4 GR22 a), required + documented | **8 bytes — one .NET managed reference on the 64-bit runtime this compiler targets — and the SAME amount for every one of the §13.18.60.2 general format's eight writable shapes.** GR22 a) expressly permits an implementation to differ per shape (“not necessarily the same for every object reference”) and COBOL.NET does not take that latitude: the descriptor (kind · name · FACTORY · ONLY) is a COMPILE-TIME fact that selects the emitted C# reference type — `CobolObject?`, the class's type, its `__FACTORY` sibling, or the interface — and every one of those is a single managed reference at run time. **Alignment: none** (the item 205 rule). **Where the 8 bytes are observable:** `FUNCTION BYTE-LENGTH` of the item is 8 (§15.14.4 rule 1); and because §13.18.60.3 SR14 admits the item as an elementary item subordinate to a type declaration with the STRONG phrase, a strongly-typed group COUNTS those 8 positions in its size (`PIC X(3)` + one reference = 11). In that group's character image the 8 positions are the D-SLOT placeholder — **eight SPACES, never the reference, whether the reference is NULL or not** — the group-image determination of DOC-A.1-56 (kb/Work PB244), and it is the one image every consumer of the group's characters reads: DISPLAY, and a MOVE to a receiver that is not strongly typed (§14.9.25.4 GR4, “no conversion of data”). A MOVE between two strongly-typed groups of the same type (§14.9.25.3 SR2) transfers the reference itself, so the receiving group's reference identifies the same object. §13.18.60.3 SR15 keeps the item out of the file section, so the placeholder never reaches a file record. ⚠ A STRING statement naming such a group as a sending item compiles and then stops at run time (the Tier-C whole-group refusal) instead of being rejected at compile time or reading this image — kb/Work PB1527. | `conformance:2002/pb496_object_reference_storage`; `conformance:2023/pb61_length_byte_length_rule_branches` |

row: | DOC-A.1-217 | **USAGE PROGRAM-POINTER clause — alignment, size, and representation of data; and allowable languages**, §13.18.60.4 GR24, required + documented | GR24 leaves four things to the implementor and this determination answers all four. **ALIGNMENT: none** (the item 205 rule). **SIZE: 8 character positions** — `FUNCTION BYTE-LENGTH` of the item is 8, the width shared with POINTER / FUNCTION-POINTER / OBJECT REFERENCE / INDEX (`PointerImage.Width`), and a strongly-typed group (§13.18.60.3 SR14) counts those 8 positions in its size. **REPRESENTATION:** the VALUE is the addressed program's externalized identity — the name of the OUTERMOST program identified by the externalized program-name in its PROGRAM-ID paragraph (§8.4.3.13.4 GR2) — held in the readonly record struct `ProgramPointer(string? Name)` (`src/Cobol.Net.Runtime/Control/ProgramPointer.cs`) and resolved and activated through the ONE run-unit `ProgramTable`, exactly as a CALL by name is; the predefined address NULL is the null name (§8.4.3.10.4 GR3, the NULL program address), and two program-pointers are equal when they name the same program, compared case-insensitively, or are both NULL. What its 8 STORAGE positions hold depends on who reads the bytes, each answer already pinned: as a BY CONTENT argument's record, the address token `PointerImage` defines (DOC-A.1-216); inside a strongly-typed group's character image, the D-SLOT placeholder — eight SPACES, whatever the value (DOC-A.1-56). **ALLOWABLE LANGUAGES: COBOL only.** GR24's second paragraph admits “another language for which the implementor has declared support for access by program pointers”, and this implementation declares none: a non-COBOL program has no run-unit registration, so `SET … TO ADDRESS OF PROGRAM` naming one takes §8.4.3.13.4 GR4 — EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND and the predefined address NULL — never an undefined outcome. | `conformance:2023/pb61_length_byte_length_rule_branches`; `conformance:2002/program_pointer`; `conformance:2002/pb460_set_program_pointer_effect`; `conformance:2002/l1c23_program_address_outermost`; `conformance:2002/pb970_pointer_by_content_storage_image`; `conformance:2002/pb244_pointer_group_transfer`; `conformance:2002/w59h_non_cobol_names_not_found` |

row: | DOC-A.1-218 | **USE statement — action taken after the USE procedure when the I-O status value indicates a fatal exception condition**, §14.9.49.4 GR7 c) and GR12 c) → §9.1.13.1, required + documented | **COBOL.NET CONTINUES the run unit.** §9.1.13.1 offers two actions (“The implementor may either continue or terminate the execution of the run unit”) and the standard does not choose; CLAUDE.md rule 1 takes GnuCOBOL's, which continues after an applicable error declarative. When the USE procedure for a fatal I-O status (first digit 3, 4 or 7, or an implementor-defined 9x value — '90' and '91', fatal per DOC-A.1-110) returns, control is transferred to the end of the input-output statement that produced the status, unless that statement's rules define other behaviour (§9.1.13.1) — a MERGE or SORT follows its own rules (GR7 a) / GR12 a); the §3 SORT/MERGE implicit-transfer determination) — and any NOT AT END or NOT INVALID KEY phrase of that statement is ignored. The answer is the same at every edition and whether or not a FILE STATUS clause is specified. **COBOL.NET does NOT “specify otherwise” under §14.6.13.1.3 rule 3**, so when checking for the EC-I-O exception condition IS enabled (`>>TURN EC-I-O CHECKING ON`, 2002+) the fatal-exception rules that follow rule 3 apply after the §9.1.13 processing: once the declarative completes normally, the run unit is terminated abnormally (rule 5 for a format 3 USE that names the condition, rule 7 after a format 1 USE procedure), and a `RESUME` executed in the declarative continues instead (NOTE 1 / NOTE 2). The checked and unchecked outcomes are therefore the standard's own split on the checking state, both read from this one determination: the unchecked program's plain `__IoCheck` (`DispatchEmitter.EmitUseMachinery`) has no fatal arm, and the checked program's `EcEmitter.EmitIoCheckEc` ends in the §14.6.13.1.3 termination. | `conformance:2002/pb344_use_mode_read_exception`; `conformance:2023/pb344_use_mode_read_exception`; `conformance:2023/pb141_resume_io` |

PB322 determination E REFUTED AS A CODE DEFECT: E says the two hooks are 'two different behaviours selected by a directive the rule does not mention'. §14.6.13.1.3 rule 3 routes a fatal EC-I-O condition through §9.1.13 and THEN, unless the implementor specifies otherwise, through rules 4-8, which key exactly on whether checking is enabled (5/7 terminate after the declarative; 8 leaves the unchecked case to the implementor). Rule-1 precedence: ISO controls the checked arm (rule 3's default, not overridden); the unchecked arm and §9.1.13.1's continue/terminate are latitude -> GnuCOBOL continues after an error declarative (its default error handler, which terminates, runs only when no declarative and no FILE STATUS applies — PB322's quoted cobc/codegen.c 11091-11092, verified in tests/external/gnucobol-3.2.tar.xz cobc/codegen.c:11040-11092). row: | DOC-A.1-219 | **User-defined words — whether extended letters may be specified in user-defined words externalized to the operating environment**, §8.3.2.2, required + documented | **Yes.** From COBOL 2002 on, an extended letter (§8.1.3.2 GR4: the Annex B repertoire, less the basic letters) may appear in ANY user-defined word, and an externalized one is no exception — a program-name, class-name, interface-name, method-name, property-name, function-name, prototype-name, or the name of an EXTERNAL data item or file. The externalized name keeps the extended letter as written, in the UTF-16 repertoire (DOC-A.1-213's national representation), and is matched at run time exactly as a basic-letter name is: case-insensitively, by the §8.1.3.2 GR4 b) uppercase/lowercase correspondence. The standard leaves the answer to the implementor, and CLAUDE.md rule 1's precedence takes GnuCOBOL's, which accepts extended characters in user-defined words, program-names included; the §5 A.4.6 Extended letters claim requires them in the words themselves. At COBOL-85 there are no extended letters, so such a character is a lexical error there. ⚠ **Today every edition rejects an extended letter in ANY user-defined word, externalized or not** — the lexer's COBOL-word class `NAME_BODY` / `NAME_TAIL` is ASCII-only (kb/Work PB1402), which also contradicts the A.4.6 claim. | — |

record.notes: cite.py --check A.1 'User-defined words (whether extended letters may be specified in user-defined words externalized to the operating environment). This item is required.' -> OK §A.1 219); cite.py --check 8.3.2.2 'The implementor shall specify whether extended letters may be specified in user-defined words externalized to the operating environment.' -> OK §8.3.2.2 2); cite.py --find 'extended letter' -> §8.1.3.1 (Table 1: 'Additional characters for use in the formation of user-defined words, as specified in Annex B') and §8.1.3.2 4) (the Annex B set). Determination: YES. ISO does not control (it requires only that the implementor specify); precedence -> GnuCOBOL, which admits extended (non-ASCII) characters in COBOL words and encodes them into C symbol names for program-ids (verified: tests/external/gnucobol-3.2.tar.xz cobc/scanner.l:978 word rule admits \x80-\xFF bytes in every COBOL word; libcob/call.c:701-789 cob_encode_program_id / cob_encode_invalid_chars encode the non-C characters of a PROGRAM-ID); coherence with the §5 A.4.6 'Extended letters — Claimed' disposition and §2 row 38 also points to YES, and .NET metadata names and file names carry UTF-16 letters, so no host constraint forces NO. Documenting 'no' would document the wrong behaviour PB1535 forbids (it falls out of the ASCII-only lexer, which also rejects NON-externalized words). DIVERGES: the compiler rejects every extended letter in every user-defined word at every edition (probe below), so the YES determination is not implemented; the 85 rejection is correct. Witness needed when PB1402 lands: a 2002 golden with an extended-letter PROGRAM-ID called by name across two separately compiled units and an EXTERNAL item shared by an extended-letter name, plus an 85 negative.
